en: One who is about to perform the *pravargya* rite—on the new moon day, the full moon day, during the bright fortnight, or on an auspicious day—shall perform the propitiatory rite (*śānti*) with the section beginning "Homage to speech" (*namo vāce*). Having placed a fuel-stick (*samidh*) made of *vaikaṅkata*, *khadira*, or *vaiṇava* wood, he offers four spoonfuls (*caturgṛhīta*) with the verse "They harness the mind" (*yuñjate manaḥ*). He should not offer for one who has already been consecrated (*dīkṣita*). With this same verse, he should either place a thorny fuel-stick or recite it over such a stick. Or else, with the formula "Thee, belonging to the god" (*devasya tvā*), he places a fuel-stick made of *khadira*, *udumbara*, *vaikaṅkata*, or *vaiṇava* wood.

Taking up a spade that is a fathom or a cubit in length, speckled, and sharpened on both ends, he consecrates it with the mantra, "Thou art a spade; thou art no woman. Having risen, he addresses the Brahman priest with, "Arise, O Lord of Prayer (*brahmaṇaspati*). The Brahman priest rises as well. Both recite the latter half-verse of the hymn, "May they both approach," while they take up the black antelope skin. Having dug up earth from anywhere, they carry it away. There, with the mantra, "May the Lord of Prayer go forth," they proceed eastward with the horse at their head. Alternatively, these ritual materials may be brought there within an enclosed space.

To the east of the Āhavanīya fire, there are earthen pits, each one to the north of the preceding one. To the north of the last pit, upon Darbha grass with its tips pointing eastward, he spreads a black antelope skin with its neck to the east and its hairy side upward, saying, "O divine Heaven and Earth. Having thus addressed Heaven and Earth, he strikes at the earthen pit with a spade, saying, "May I prosper today," and takes away the earth from the pit, saying, "The head of Makha. Having carried it away, saying, "For Makha thee," he pours it out upon the black antelope skin, saying, "For the head of Makha thee. He does the same for the second and the third [pits].

And having taken [the earth], he pours it out silently for a fourth time, or an unlimited amount—namely as many lumps of earth as have been obtained from the Pravargya vessels; he leaves a remainder for expiation, and the same applies to the other ritual materials.

With the words, "So much was there at the beginning," he approaches the spot dug up by a boar. With the words, "The divine ants," he approaches the mound of an anthill. With the words, "Thou art the vigor of Indra," he approaches the *pūtīka* plants. With the words, "Thou art born of Agni; thou art the seed of Prajāpati," he separately approaches the hair from the skin of a black antelope mixed with wool. Having thrown them down and gathered them together, he pours them onto the black antelope skin. He pours the five materials while reciting, "Bestow life; bestow breath. Having caused the horse to sniff them with the words, "May honey make thee sweet," the priests milk a single she-goat with a male calf around the materials that have been poured out.

All take up the Pravargya vessels. To the north of the sacrificial ground, having enclosed it with a screen, having dug out the earth, sprinkled it with water, and scattered sand, they set them down. Having first heated the boiling waters over the Gārhapatya fire, he pours them over the Pravargya vessel with the formula, "May honey make thee sweet," and mixes the vessel with them.

Furthermore, whatever other clay substances for mixing with the cauldron—such as gravel, collyrium powder, flour, and so forth—are used for the sake of firmness, he mixes them into this *pravargya* vessel. Whatever requires water, having heated it in that manner, it is performed with the *madantī* waters. No woman looks upon it, nor a *śūdra*. One should not breathe over the vessels while making them; rather, setting aside the mouth, one performs the action with a bamboo tube without breathing over it. One should not pass between the *pravargya* and the sun at any point once the *pravargya* has commenced.

When the sun has set, he desists; having desisted, he completes what remains on the following day. Having thoroughly kneaded those clods of earth and formed them into a lump with the formula, "Thou art the head of Makha," he presses it down with his two thumbs and his fingers used according to their purpose, saying, "Ye are the two feet of the sacrifice. Having divided that into three parts and made three lumps, he hands the first to the maker with the formula, "Thou art Gāyatra," the second with "Thou art Traiṣṭubha," and the third with "Thou art Jāgata"; and [he says] over the first, "I fashion thee with the Gāyatrī metre."

With three meters, he fashions three *mahāvīra* vessels of the Vāyavya type—having three elevations, five elevations, or an unlimited number of elevations—each a span in height, with upward-facing rims that are hollowed out at the top like a pouring vessel and curved inward at the middle. Having fashioned the rim (*rāsnā*) around the opening with the formula, "Thou art the girth of Makha," he makes the opening with a bamboo joint, saying, "May Aditi seize thy opening. (3)

To whatever extent he deems sufficient for the portion for the deity, for the Sviṣṭakṛt, for the Agnihotra, and for the portions to be consumed—having placed those on the sand to the north, he heats each one individually with the sunlight, saying, "Be heated by the heat of the sun. He gazes at them with the formula, "Thou art Makha," and silently [heats] the others that have pouring-spouts. With clay, he fashions two milking-vessels with handles shaped like an elephant's trunk; the Adhvaryu's vessel is larger, while the Pratiprasthātṛ's is the milking-vessel. There are two butter-pots and two curd-pots.

If the sacrifice involves the piling of the fire-altar (*agnicityā*), then when the two *rauhiṇaka* potsherds have been made circular, he coats the *gharma-iṣṭakā* and the *kulāyinī* with the remaining clay and dries them in the wind. While they are drying, they smooth them with smoothing agents. Having set fire to the dung of a stallion and other materials at the *gārhapatya* fire, he takes the first *mahāvīra* vessel with its two hooves while reciting, "Thou art the footprint of the stallion," and fumigates it both inside and out; he does the same for the other two. For the others, he does so silently. From this point onward, he should take up the *mahāvīras* only with the two hooves.

To the east of the *gārhapatya* fire, he digs a pit. Into it, having scattered the materials for baking the red vessels, he carries down the *mahāvīra* vessels one by one in order, either toward the east or toward the north, with the formula: "O God, go forward; may I attain thee. Having placed the two milking vessels to the east, the two *rauhiṇa* potsherds to the west, and the two vessels for clarified butter and curds on top, he covers them with those baking materials and smears them with clay. For the purpose of heating, he leaves a space of four finger-breadths in each direction. Having kindled tufts of *muñja* grass over the *gārhapatya* fire, [he places them] for the sake of the flame.

With the mantras beginning with *tvā*, he heats [the vessels] toward each direction one by one; or else, with all [the mantras], he heats them from all sides. These are cooked either during the day or at night. If he heats them in the evening, he approaches them in the morning; if in the morning, in the evening. With the two *maitrī* verses, "This [is] for me" and "With greatness," he attends to them while they are being cooked. When they are cooked, having taken the two stirring-sticks (*dhṛṣṭī*) with the mantra "For success, thee," he pushes away the embers with them. With the mantra "May the god Savitṛ lift thee up," he first lifts out the *mahāvīra* vessel with the two tongs (*śapha*), [saying] "not falling on the earth, [filling] the quarters and directions."

With the words "Fill [the quarters]!", he establishes it on the sand to the north; he does the same for the other two silently; the others [he places] silently; with the words "I gaze upon you with the eye of Sūrya," he gazes at them.

For a Brāhmaṇa, he pours sand around [the Mahāvīra] from left to right with the formula: "This I heap around so-and-so, the son of such-and-such, with Brahman-splendor"; for a Rājanya, he modifies it to "with the people (viśā)"; for a Vaiśya, "with cattle (paśubhiḥ). Having grasped each Mahāvīra by its two handles and placed it in the vessel, he covers it with abundant goat's milk, using these three formulas respectively: "I cover thee with the Gāyatrī metre," and so on; he covers it both inside and out, making it well-covered.

He causes it to overflow with cow's milk while the milker remains silent. Regarding the two *rauhiṇaka* potsherds and the two vessels for clarified butter and curds: if a crack or a fissure occurs, one should take a small amount from the remaining [clay], grind it, scatter it over goat’s milk, and smear that over the fissure. Then, with the two verses, "The fissure that has opened" and "Whatever [is done] apart from union," he heals it. However, if it breaks completely, one should grind those potsherds, mix them with the remaining clay, fashion [new vessels] in that manner, and heal them. This applies to the *pravargya* vessels as well.

Having bound it with a black antelope skin and hung it on a sling with the verse, "O God, go forward to the house; may I attain thee," he places it so that the wife does not see it until the performance is completed; then they perform the final pacification with the verse, "May the wind be auspicious to us."

At the time of proceeding, having performed the *pravargya* rite, they proceed with the *upasad*; or, having performed the *upasad*, they proceed with the *pravargya*. Those intending to perform it in that manner close the doors so that women do not see them; they enclose the areas where the wives move about. The *adhvaryu* sits down in front, the *hotṛ* behind him, the *prastotṛ* to the south-west, the *brahmán* and the sacrificer to the south, and the *pratiprasthātṛ* and the *āgnīdhra* to the north. Having touched water and recited the pacification formula, "Homage to speech," they murmur the *śānti*.

Having spread bundles of *muñja* grass in front of the *gārhapatya* fire, he brings down the first *mahāvīra* vessel upon them with the formula, "O God, O Fore-goer, may I attain thee!"; he brings down the other two in the same manner, and the remaining items for the *pravargya* silently right there. He arranges the materials required for the *pravargya*: the *somāsandī* is larger in form, while the *samrāḍāsandī* is smaller; there are four ladles (*srucaḥ*), of which two are *rauhiṇahavanyau* and the other two are *animne*; of these two, the larger one is the *upayamanī*, and the smaller one is the *prokṣaṇīdhānī*. There are two [cups].

There are two *sruva* ladles and two *dhṛṣṭi* spoons, equal in size to the *mahāvīra* vessel; they are cut on one side and perforated on the other, and these are called *saṃdaṃśa* tongs and *śapha* hooves. There is a thick-pointed peg for milking the *gharma*, three thin-pointed pegs for the calves and so forth—these are called *avatsa-śaṅku* (calves' pegs)—and six pieces of wood for those who walk on foot; all these are made of *udumbara* wood. The fuel-stick is of *vikaṅkata* wood, the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) are of *vikaṅkata* wood, and there are thirteen logs of firewood: some of *palāśa*, some of *veṇu* (bamboo), some of *vikaṅkata*, some of *khadira*, some of *arka*, and some of *udumbara*.

Or [the fans] may be made of *śamī* wood; there are three fans with handles the length of an arm, having white and black hair, and made of black antelope skin. The handles are made of bamboo or *udumbara* wood. There is a hundred-māna weight of silver and gold. There are two Veda-strainers, one with an intact tip and one with a cut tip. There are two binding-cords and three branch-ropes; these are made of *muñja* grass, unhusked, and consist of the flour of the two *rauhiṇa* cakes. There are abundant cuttings of *muñja* grass and sand from the mounds. The two *pavitra* strainers, made of *muñja* or *darbha* grass, are placed to the north of the *gārhapatya* fire.

Having scraped [the ground] with the wooden sword (sphya), sprinkled it with water, and scattered sand, one should prepare a circular mound for the Pravargya vessel, one span high, to the north of the Āhavanīya fire; likewise, one should prepare a mound for the Udvāsana vessel to the north of the hall, square and with a runoff channel. Having thus prepared three mounds, the remaining sand should be placed in the northern half. Then, having consecrated the sprinkling waters (prokṣaṇī), [the Adhvaryu says]: "O Brahman, we shall proceed with the Pravargya; O Hotṛ, recite for the Gharma; O Agnīdh, place the two Dākṣiṇa cakes on the fire; O Pratiprasthātṛ..."
"O Prastotṛ, perform the Pravargya; sing the Sāmans!"—thus he issues the summons to the Brahmā and the others.

Then Brahmā, having whispered "yajuryuktam" (the one joined with the Yajus), loudly issues the command: "O, proceed, accompanied by Indra! The Adhvaryu, being thus impelled, sprinkles all the Pravargya materials three times each with the *madantī* waters, using the formula "For Yama thee! For Makha thee!", so that he may reach the other materials. Having sprinkled them, he spreads them out. Being prompted, the Hotṛ begins with "brahma jajñānam" and recites the hymn; having chanted as far as the *ṛgāvāna*, he should pause. The Āgnīdhra places the two *rauhiṇa* cakes upon the fire.

The Pratiprasthātṛ, having prepared the clarified butter like a *darvihoma*, places the curd over the fire; having carried the *samrāḍ-āsandī* around the front of the Āhavanīya, he sets it down either to the east or to the north of the *rāja-āsandī*. Upon it, he spreads a black antelope skin with the neck toward the east and the hair upward; upon that, he places the two great *mahāvīra* vessels lying thereon. Taking the *apracaraṇī* (the non-functioning vessel), the *sthalashanku*, the calf-pins, and the forked ropes, he passes to the south of the Hotṛ, goes forward, and brings them in through the southern door.

To the south, for the Hotṛ’s inspection, he drives in a peg for the mother [cow] near the southern door; to the south of the eastern door-post, a peg for the calf of the Gharma-cow; and to the south of the western door-post, a peg for the she-goat. Having driven in a peg for the he-goat to the north inside [the shed], he stretches out the ropes with forked ends there. At this time, they milk the cows while they are tied up until the removal of the vessel. Having piled up three mounds of earth, he places the cooked curds and chips of wood to the north of the Āhavanīya fire, as well as a fuel-stick of *vikaṅkata* wood. 8.

Then the Adhvaryu, having grasped the Mahāvīra vessel intended for use with two tongs, holding it in his left hand, and having wiped its top with the edge [of the ladle], anoints it once with clarified butter taken with the *sruva* from the *ājyasthālī*. He offers seven oblations of breath (*prāṇāhuti*) into the Gārhapatya fire without pausing and continuously, saying "To breath, svāhā! and so on, or eleven; then he anoints that Mahāvīra with the remainder of the butter from the *sruva*, saying, "May the god Savitṛ anoint you with honey," over the earth.

At this time, while [the Adhvaryu] says, "Protect us with austerity," the Pratiprasthātṛ hides a silver *śatamāna* coin in the *khara* mound used for heating. Taking blades of *muñja* grass, he kindles the tips of the southern blades on the Gārhapatya fire with the formula, "Thou art flame" (*arcis asi*). With the formula, "Thou art light" (*śociḥ asi*), he kindles the roots of the northern blades with the tips of those [southern ones]. With the formula, "Thou art radiance" (*jyotis asi*), he kindles the roots of the southern blades with the roots of those [northern ones]. With the formula, "Thou art austerity" (*tapaḥ asi*), he kindles the tips of the northern blades with the roots of those [southern ones]. Having placed them intertwined upon the *śatamāna* coin, he sets down the Mahāvīra vessel over them with the formula, "Sit together" (*saṃsīdasva*).

He deposits [the Mahāvīra] with the formula, "They anoint him... He fills it with clarified butter with the formula, "Unassailable in front... With these formulas, according to their respective characteristics, the sacrificer, without touching the Mahāvīra, establishes the directions by means of a span. To the north, he touches the earth with the formula, "Thou art the horse of Manu, O thou of many sons. Having taken up the two fire-sticks with the formula, "For success thee," the Adhvaryu and the Pratiprasthātṛ, having drawn out embers toward the north from the Gārhapatya fire with the formula, "O Agni, heat is thine," and having placed them around it clockwise with the formula, "Ye are piled, ye are piled around," they lay down thirteen enclosing sticks (paridhis). 9.

With the formula "Thou art the measure," the Adhvaryu lays down two [stones] facing east; with "Thou art the counter-measure," the Pratiprasthātṛ [lays down] two facing north. In this manner, two by two, the Adhvaryu uses each preceding mantra and the Pratiprasthātṛ each succeeding one. With the formula "Thou art the intermediate space of the atmosphere," the Adhvaryu alone lays down the thirteenth stone on the south side. Having covered it from above with a golden disk (rukma) with the formula "Protect the sky from heat," he worships it with the three verses beginning with "With these songs. He lays down each individual stone with the formulas beginning with "Thou art the Gāyatra."

He takes up the fans; then, bending his right knee, he thrice fans him [the Mahāvīra] upward with them, saying "Honey! Honey! Having himself taken the first of these, he hands the middle one to the Pratiprasthātṛ and the other to the Āgnīdhra. Saying "Honey! Honey!", they go three times around the Mahāvīra clockwise, fanning it upward, starting from the Āgnīdhra, with the syllable *praṇava* (Om). Having sat down according to their respective places, they remain silent, kindling the fire while anointing the Mahāvīra, until it is fully ablaze.

He takes up a gold piece weighing a hundred mānas with the verse, "With those [rays] by which you released the swallowed quail. Recognizing the signal of the Hotṛ, the Adhvaryu consecrates the Mahāvīra vessel with the Anuvāka beginning, "Ten rays toward the east; ten thou shinest to the south," and continuing, "O Aśvins, grant us speech full of wealth. Recognizing the signal, they lift up the fanning fans. Recognizing the signal, "The dappled one has caused the dawns to shine at their head," and saying, "The Gharma has shone," they go around it three times again in the opposite direction, fanning with the fans as they went.

Having taken it back and carried it around the front of the Āhavanīya fire, the Adhvaryu places it on the Samrāj seat in the morning with the formula, "Svāhā! To thee for the rays of Sūrya," and in the evening with, "Svāhā! To thee for the constellations. Having stood in their respective places, all the officiating priests and the sacrificer, reciting the verse, "I have seen the guardian," gaze at the Mahāvīra vessel. The Adhvaryu worships the Gārhapatya fire with the verse, "Thou, O Agni, art the lord of the house," while the Pratiprasthātṛ stands behind him. He causes the wife to recite, "May Tvaṣṭṛ make thee possessed of offspring," and issues the command, "O Agnīdh, place the two Daurhiṇa cakes. 10.

In the forenoon, the Āgnīdhra places two *rauhiṇa* cakes, which have been spread with a base of butter and sprinkled over, upon the southern and northern junctions of the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*), while the two offering-ladles (*srucau*) are turned toward the east; some say they are placed facing west in the afternoon. Having taken the rope with the formula "By the impulse of the god... and having consecrated the rope with the formula "Thou art the girdle of Aditi," the Adhvaryu goes out by the eastern door and calls the cow that yields the *gharma* milk, saying three times in a whisper, "O *Iḍā*, come! O Aditi, come! O Sarasvatī, come! and three times aloud according to her name, "Come, so-and-so!"

Having returned, the Adhvaryu, the Āgnīdhra, and the Pratiprasthātṛ take the rope and the milking vessel at the source; having led [the cow] out by the southern door, the Adhvaryu binds the dewlap of the Gharma-milker around its neck with the rope, saying, "Thou art the turban of Aditi"; [he binds] the calf with the words, "Vāyu is thy bone, the goat thy flesh. He lets the calf loose with the words, "May Pūṣan let thee loose. Having consecrated the Gharma-milker with the verse, "That breast of thine which is inexhaustible," he takes the calf, yokes it, and says, "O Ustra, guard the Gharma!"

"May Bṛhaspati sit near you," he says as he sits down. "Ye are the liberal Dānavas," with these words he touches the udders. Recognizing them with the formula, "With the ten [fingers] of Vivasvat," he causes them to swell for the Aśvins with the formula, "Swell for the milker who is more generous. At this time, the Pratiprasthātṛ silently gives two portions of milk from the goat to the Agnīdhra for the one who is less generous. Having returned by the same way they came, the Adhvaryu takes up the two hoof-marks with the formulas, "Thou art Gāyatra; thou art Triṣṭubh," and the Pratiprasthātṛ takes up the supporting-stand with the formula, "Thou art Jāgata; come near."

The Āgnīdhra enters [the ritual space] with the recognition formula, "O milker of cows! The Adhvaryu awaits the milk being brought forward, saying, "Come hither with a portion of vigor! (ŚB 4.5.2.11).

With the formula, "O Indra and Aśvins," he pours the cow's milk into the Mahāvīra vessel. With the formula, "Svāhā! You, by the rays of the sun," he stands worshipping the rising steam. With the formula, "You are the honey oblation," the Pratiprasthātṛ stands worshipping the rising steam of the goat's milk. With the formula, "By the heat of the sun," [the Pratiprasthātṛ] stands worshipping the rising steam. With the formula, "I enclose you for Heaven and Earth," the Adhvaryu encloses the Mahāvīra with a pair of tongs. Having wiped it with the *veda*-grass, with the formula, "I support you with the intermediate space," the Pratiprasthātṛ supports it with the supporting-stand. [For] the gods...

Saying "Tva," he rises; saying "Thou art splendor, follow after splendor," he brings [the fuel] from the east. Having murmured, "May Agni protect me from the earth, Vāyu from the atmosphere, Sūrya from the sky; do not harm me, O toucher of heaven," he recites the five names of the winds—beginning with "To the ocean, to thee, to Vāta, Svāhā!"—without taking breath as he proceeds. Then he recites the seven subsequent ones, beginning with "To Agni accompanied by the Vasus, Svāhā! and the remaining five for the sake of the option. At this time, the Pratiprasthātṛ offers the southern oblation, [saying] "Light."

He offers with "By the banner" in the morning and with "By the night" in the evening. Having stepped around behind the Āhavanīya fire toward the south, he looks at the Brahman priest with "Seated in the south, [protect] all the quarters. He looks at the Hotṛ priest seated to the west with "He has sacrificed here for all the gods," and he looks at the Gharma vessel with "Of the Gharma consecrated by Svāhā. After the call for the *āśrāvaṇa* and the response, he issues the direction: "Recite the offering-verse for the Gharma! He proceeds with the highest voice, saying "O Aśvins, drink the Gharma," and he makes the offering when the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered; he makes the second offering when the *anuvaṣaṭ* is uttered with "Svāhā! To Indra!"

With the verse, "O Aśvins, you have drunk the Gharma," he pays homage to the offered Gharma. With the remainder of the section beginning, "Homage to Heaven, homage to Earth," the sacrificer pays homage to the Mahāvīra pot being held over the Āhavanīya fire; the Pratiprasthātṛ then fills it with curds mixed with boiled milk. 12.

The sacrificer recites over the flowing [milk] "For nourishment, swell up! either in a low voice with "For me," or then he causes it to flow toward the quarters: with "For brilliance, thee! toward the east; with "For splendor, thee! toward the south; with "For power, thee! toward the west; with "For prosperity, thee! toward the north. Having stepped back and poured the remainder of the milk from the Mahāvīra into the supporting vessel, and having placed a silver *śatamāna* coin on the mound for the removal [of the vessel], he places the Mahāvīra upon it with the formula, "Thou art Gharma; may not the wind blow thee away."

While the Āditya-skanda sacrifice is being performed, having touched water and taken six chips of Udumbara wood, he causes [the ghee] to drip from each one of them onto the supporting substance with the formula, "To Pūṣan, the arrow-shooter, svāhā! He lets it drip in the eastern half of the Āhavanīya fire and places it so that it touches the middle enclosing-stick (paridhi) while being anointed within; in the same way, with the second chip, he causes it to drip with "To the pressing-stones, svāhā! and places it as before; likewise with the third, and with the fourth in the middle with "To the Pratiribhas, svāhā!"

With "To Heaven and Earth, svāhā! he offers on the west side; then he covers this upward-pointing wick in the ashes. In the same way, with the fifth [offering], "To the Fathers who drink the Gharma, svāhā! he places this outward-pointing wick on the southern enclosing-stick so that it touches it. Then, having mixed all the residues together, he takes a portion from the supporting-wood and finally offers the sixth [oblation] on the northern part with "To Rudra, whose priest is Rudra, svāhā! Then, without looking back, he carries this out through a gap to the north of the hall along with that [waste].

Saying "Go," he casts [the wood] away; having touched water and sprinkled the remaining wood-chips with water, the Pratiprasthātṛ throws them into the Āhavanīya fire as before. The Adhvaryu offers the second Rauhiṇa cake with the formula, "You have carried me across; protect me from night and from day. In the morning, he should place a fuel-stick of *vikaṅkata* wood on the fire with the formula, "You have carried me across; protect me from day and from night"; in the evening, [he does so] with the formula, "You have carried me across; protect me from night and from day. (13)

From the remainder, he offers the Agnihotra with the supporting ladle (*upayamana*), saying: "Agni is light, light is Agni, svāhā! in the evening; "Sūrya is light, light is Sūrya, svāhā! in the morning; or he may offer it at both times with the *vyāhṛtis*, or silently. Having invited [the priests] to partake of the remainder, saying, "The oblation is offered, the oblation is honey," the sacrificer alone eats it directly. The Hotṛ and the others eat by smelling it. The Āgnīdhra cleanses the supporting ladle in the pit for the remnants (*ucchiṣṭakhara*) and places it within the altar with its opening facing east. Into that, he throws two coins of gold and silver weighing a hundred *mānas*.

Having poured out the boiling waters, they purify themselves with those waters containing gold, while the sacrificer is the sixth, using the four verses beginning "Golden-hued, pure... Having taken clarified butter from the butter-pot with the dipping-spoon, they offer the expiations for the *pravargya* rite with these two sections beginning "To Prāṇa, svāhā! To Pūṣan, svāhā! Then, having drawn water from the supporting-stand and placed all the *gharma* vessels therein, he touches it and issues the command: "Recite for the *gharma* being set down," [up to] "In whom the seven Vasus..."

Having recognized this, they carry that very vessel of milk around the front of the Āhavanīya fire and place it on the south side upon the black antelope skin on the *samrāḍ-āsandī* throne, with its opening facing east, saying: "Svāhā! To thee for the rays of the sun! thus at dawn; and "Svāhā! To thee for the constellations! thus in the evening. Having recognized [the cow] with the words, "Eat grass, O inviolable one, at all times," and having released the Gharma-milking cow, they perform the propitiatory rite (*śānti*) at this time with the final Anuvāka, beginning with "May the wind blow auspiciously for us. Thus for three nights.
For six nights or twelve nights, they perform the Pravargya and Upasad rites every morning and evening.

Having consumed the *pravargya* offering, one should not eat meat for a year or for four months; one should not approach a woman, nor drink from an earthen vessel, nor should anyone drink his leavings. "This sharpens his very brilliance (*tejas*)," so says the *Brāhmaṇa*. One performs the *pravargya* at the *agniṣṭoma*, but one should not perform it at the *ukthya*. One performs it at the *viśvajit* sacrifice when all the *pṛṣṭha*-stotras are employed, but one should not perform it at one's first sacrifice. Alternatively, one may perform it for a *śrotriya* who has studied the Vedas, for a wicked Brāhmaṇa, and for one who desires spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*).

Intending to remove the *pravargya* vessels, he gives a goat to the *Āgnīdhra*, a four-year-old cow to the *Brahman*, the *gharma*-milking cow to the *Hotṛ*, and two gold pieces weighing a hundred *mānas* to the *Adhvaryu*. Then, having performed the preliminary pacification (*pūrvaśānti*) and spread grass in front of the *Āhavanīya* fire, he places all the *parigharmya* implements upon the *samrāḍ-āsandi* throne. Then the *Āgnīdhra*, having placed the two *khara* mounds—the one for the *pravṛñjana* and the one for the removal—into a vessel, sets them down to the north of the *samrāḍ-āsandi*. Having placed the *ucchiṣṭa-khara* mound into another vessel and carried it out through the southern door, he sets it down.

He places it in the *mārjālīya* area; having returned by the same way he came, the *pratiprasthātṛ* covers the wife’s eyes with a cloth whose fringes point north. Having melted the clarified butter over the *gārhapatya* fire and purified it, and having taken four spoonfuls into a ladle made of *udumbara* wood, he takes three handfuls of fire-sticks together with their roots. Having kindled one of them at the *āhavanīya* fire, he holds it at the height of his mouth. Into that, the *adhvaryu* offers the first oblation of the *gharma* with the formula, "O Gharma, that heat of thine which is in heaven... He then kindles another stick and, having cast the first one into the *āhavanīya*, [offers the second].

With the verse, "O Gharma, that which is yours in the intermediate space," he offers the second oblation at the height of the navel; likewise, having kindled it again, with the verse, "O Gharma, that which is yours on the earth," he offers the third oblation at the height of the knee. Or rather, having opened his fists, he offers three oblations in the Āhavanīya fire according to their respective locations. Having closed the doors and taken up the Pravargya vessel, they go out by the eastern door with the two verses, "May Anumati favor us today" and "Do thou, O Anumati. The Pratiprasthātṛ leads the wife with a garment. Having stepped onto the Mahāvedi, he issues the command: "O Prastotṛ, chant the Sāman! 15.

The sacrificer together with his wife and all the officiating priests perform the *nidhana* of the *sāman* three times; it is known from the tradition that "each individual person performs the *nidhana*. Having reached the first [spot] with the words, "For the protection of heaven (*divas tvā paraspāyai*"), they proceed eastward to the middle region while performing the second *nidhana* with the words, "For the protection of the Brahman (*brahmaṇas tvā paraspāyai*"); having reached the location of the *uparava* holes, they perform the third *nidhana* with the words, "For the protection of the vital breath (*prāṇasya tvā paraspāyai*)."

Stepping forward for the third time, having reached the northern side of the *uttaravedi* at the place where the [fire] is to be removed, and having established the *samrāḍ-āsandi* throne, he issues the command: "O Prastotṛ, chant the Vārṣāhara Sāman; chant the Iṣṭāhotrīya Sāman. They reach the *nidhana* of the Iṣṭāhotrīya as before, but not that of the Vārṣāhara. Taking a water-pitcher, he goes around the entire *parigharmya* vessel on the *uttaravedi*, sprinkling it with a continuous stream while reciting, "Thou art the leaping one," and having set down the pitcher, he recites, "And bring us peace."

Sprinkling water three times, he goes around it in the opposite direction; with the words, "The navel of the cosmic order (ṛta) has four corners," he touches the northern navel; with the words, "The seat of all life," he pours out the two mounds to the north of the navel; with the words, "Drive away hatred, drive away [enmity]," he pours out the mound for the remains at the Mārjālīya fire-altar. Having washed his hands and spread a black antelope skin on the northern altar (uttaravedi), having placed gold upon it, and having scattered the flour of the Rauhiṇa cakes, pieces of Muñja grass, and sand over it, he [prepares] the *pracaraṇī* ladle with the words, "O God, go forward; may I attain thee."

He brings down the Mahāvīra [vessel] with the formula, "Thou art the milk of the great ones. He fills it with curds mixed with honey. In the same way he fills the other two, whether they are the eastern and western or the southern and northern ones, silently. The others become like the disk of the sun. Alternatively, for the *pracaraṇī* [ladle], he uses the formula, "Thou art the milk of the great ones," for the clarified butter; "Thou art the light of the trees, the essence of the plants," for the honey; and "Thee, the vigorous one, we pour out, O vigorous ones," for the curds. In the same way for the other two as well: clarified butter in the first, honey in the second, and curds in the third.

"O Gharma, this is your food, this is your sediment"—with these words, he fills those [vessels] that have openings for pouring with curds mixed with honey, so that they are not empty; thus it is known. 16.

Alternatively, one who desires to fashion it in the form of a person should do so, following the same procedure up to the removal of the *pracaraṇī* ladle. That [wooden board] becomes the head; he places a Veda-grass mat with its tip pointing eastward upon it, which becomes the crest-lock. On both sides of the head are the two milking-pots (*dogdhre*), which are the ears; the *prokṣaṇī* vessel is the mouth; the two *sruva* spoons are the nostrils; the two *sruva* spoons on either side are the eyes; the pot for clarified butter (*ājyasthālī*) is the neck; the two stirring-sticks (*dhṛṣṭī*) are the collarbones; the two hooves on either side are the shoulders; the two *rauhiṇa* offering-vessels are the forearms; the eastern tethering-post is the back; and the two fans on either side are the ribs.

The third fanning-rod is the chest; the supporting-wood (upayamana) is the middle part, the belly; on both sides are the spades, the hips; on both sides are the two pegs, the thighs; in the middle is the third, the penis; on both sides are the two Rauhiṇa-pans, the heels. Upon that he places everything made of cord; these are the entrails. He scatters the flour of the Rauhiṇa-cakes all around; these are the marrow. Having released the Veda-bundle, he strews it over [the altar]; these are the sinews. He covers it with Avakā-plants and grass; these are the veins. With the formula, "O Gharma, this is your food, this is your soil," he pours the remainder of the curds [over it].

Having wiped [the vessel] with honey-mixed [curds], he pours that flesh between the two thighs; he sprinkles it all over with curds mixed with honey—that is the blood. He covers it with a black antelope skin, with the neck toward the east and the hair upward. Having loosened the Samrāj-throne, he places it on top; thus there is sovereignty. 17.

Regarding those who state that the ritual procedure on the *uttaravedi* is constant, [the text says]: "One should remove [the Gharma] from the *uttaravedi* for one desiring splendor"—this is stated in the Brāhmaṇa. One may do as one pleases; birds should not settle upon it once it has been removed. Until the carrying forward of the fire (*agnipraṇayana*), some prescribe the sprinkling of water with a water-pitcher around it. He worships it with the mantra: "Thou art delight, the divine Gandharva. The sacrificer and the Adhvaryu [worship] with: "The tawny bull has bellowed," and [the sacrificer continues]: "O God Gharma, this I, a man, [salute] men."

Having circumambulated to the right and cleansed himself on the mound for the remnants, he returns without looking back. Having worshipped the sun with the verse, "We have risen above the darkness," he offers oblations into the Gārhapatya fire with the two verses, "Upwards that light" and "The bright [face]," or he worships it, according to some teachers. He worships the Āhavanīya fire with the verse, "This very one," or the Gārhapatya. They proceed to the subsequent pacification rite with the verse, "May the wind blow auspiciously for us. They proceed. Thus ends the thirteenth question.
